L52@P3: Abstract
L53@P3: The rapid development and wide application of distributed network systems have made network
L54@P3: security – especially access control and data privacy – ever more important. Blockchain
L55@P3: technology offers features such as decentralization, high confidence, and tamper-resistance, which
L56@P3: are advantages to solving auditability, resource consumption, scalability, central authority, and
L57@P3: trust issues – all of which are challenges for network access control by traditional mechanisms.
L58@P3: This document presents general information for blockchain access control systems from the views
L59@P3: of blockchain system properties, components, functions, and supports for access control policy
L60@P3: models. Considerations for implementing blockchain access control systems are also included.

L97@P5: Executive Summary
L98@P5: Access control is concerned with determining the allowed activities of legitimate users and
L99@P5: mediating every attempt by a user to access a resource in the system. The objectives of an access
L100@P5: control system are often described in terms of protecting system resources against inappropriate
L101@P5: or undesired user access. From a business perspective, this objective could just as well be described
L102@P5: in terms of the optimal sharing of information. As current information systems and network
L103@P5: architectures evolve to be more lightweight, pervasive, and interactive – such as the cloud and
L104@P5: Internet of Things (IoT) – there is need for an access control mechanism to support the
L105@P5: requirements of decentralization, scalability, and trust for accessing objects, all of which are
L106@P5: challenging for traditional mechanisms.
L107@P5: Blockchains are tamper-evident and tamper-resistant cryptographically linked blocks of data
L108@P5: (which create digital ledgers) implemented in a distributed fashion (i.e., without a central
L109@P5: repository) and usually without a central authority (i.e., a bank, company, or government). It uses
L110@P5: replicated, shared, and synchronized digital blocks between the users of a private or public
L111@P5: distributed computer network located in different sites or organizations. Blockchain can be utilized
L112@P5: for access control systems as a trustable alternative for a single entity/organization or a member of
L113@P5: a large-scale system to enforce access control policies. The robust, distributed nature of blockchain
L114@P5: technology can overcome the limitations of traditional access control systems in a decentralized
L115@P5: and efficient way. It is supported by the following infrastructural properties that are not included
L116@P5: in traditional access control mechanisms unless specifically implemented:
L117@P5: • Tamper-evident and tamper-resistant design prevents the alteration of access control data
L118@P5: (i.e., attributes, policy rules, environment conditions, and access requests) and access
L119@P5: control logs (i.e., request permissions and previous access control data) and reduces the
L120@P5: probability of frauds.
L121@P5: • The control of authorization processing is decentralized, and the storage of access control
L122@P5: data/logs has no single point of failure, thus providing more system tolerance and
L123@P5: availability.
L124@P5: • The traceability of blocks allows access control data/logs and system states to be seen and
L125@P5: tracked.
L126@P5: • The execution of arbitrary programs in smart contracts allows for controls on distributed
L127@P5: access control data and authorization processes.
L128@P5: • Consensus mechanisms and protocols jointly regulate the participating access control
L129@P5-6: entities/organizations in determining policy rules through blocks or smart contracts. NIST IR 8403 BLOCKCHAIN FOR ACCESS CONTROL SYSTEMS
